source_caption:
Martin Scorsese’s The Aviator (2004) is a fascinating portrait of Howard Hughes — a man whose ambition seemed limitless, but whose own obsessions slowly became his greatest enemy.

It’s not the kind of film most people associate with Scorsese, but you can still feel his fingerprints all over it: larger-than-life characters, incredible attention to detail, spectacular set pieces, and a deeply flawed man at the center of it all.

Leonardo DiCaprio completely disappears into Hughes. This is far removed from the young star we saw in Titanic. He captures Hughes’ confidence, ambition, brilliance, and, eventually, his paranoia in a performance that feels both powerful and unsettling.

And the spectacle is incredible. Plane crashes, dangerous test flights, Hollywood productions, and Hughes’ battle against Pan Am all give the film a huge sense of scale.

But underneath all of that, The Aviator is really about a man fighting himself. Hughes keeps pushing aviation and filmmaking forward, even as his mind slowly begins to turn against him.

It’s one of Scorsese’s most ambitious films — and one of DiCaprio’s most memorable performances.

source_details.synopsis: The Aviator is a 2004 epic biographical drama film directed by Martin Scorsese and written by John Logan. It stars Leonardo DiCaprio as Howard Hughes, Cate Blanchett as Katharine Hepburn, and Kate Beckinsale as Ava Gardner. The supporting cast includes John C. Reilly, Alec Baldwin, Alan Alda and Jude Law. The film depicts the life of Howard Hughes, an aviation pioneer and director of the film Hell's Angels (1930). The film portrays his life from 1927 to 1947, when Hughes became a successful film producer and an aviation magnate while simultaneously growing more unstable due to severe obsessive–compulsive disorder (OCD).
